# Bisaya Post-Class Speech and Affective State Recognition Among Computer Science Students

**Group 3 Research Report: Second-Year Computer Science Students (pilot study)**

*Generated by `src/09_build_final_report.py` on 2026-10-12 from the outputs of the project pipeline. Every number in this report is read from a generated data file.*

## Abstract

This pilot study tested whether acoustic and prosodic features of a single, naturally spoken Bisaya word, recorded immediately after class, carry information about the speaker's independently self-reported valence and arousal.

Of 40 second-year CS participants in the Group 3 metadata, 40 had a usable recording, which meets the protocol minimum of 40; by the group's decision these are the CS2B_v2_wav_16k copies, 9 of them without a verified original recording.

From each recording's automatically located target utterance, 108 features were extracted (F0, energy, zero-crossing rate, MFCC with derivatives, spectral and temporal descriptors). Logistic regression, an RBF support-vector machine and a random forest were compared with dummy baselines under repeated, nested, participant-grouped cross-validation.

No learned model exceeded the label-permutation null after Holm correction (all adjusted p ≥ 0.05; smallest unadjusted p = 0.0060, before correcting for 9 tests). Before correction, 1 of 9 tests had p < 0.05 (Random forest on valence_2: p = 0.006). If no model carried any signal, about 0.45 such results would be expected by chance across these tests, and none survives the correction. Self-reported valence and arousal were strongly correlated (Spearman ρ = 0.72). Feature–affect correlations surviving FDR correction: 1 of 108 for valence, 0 for arousal.

No recording-configuration artefact was detectable, but the trimmed, partly edited copies analysed instead of the original recordings, and the automatic utterance localisation, add further uncertainty. Within this pilot dataset, the results do not support a claim that the system can recognise post-class affect from speech. The findings should be interpreted as a feasibility study.

## 1. Introduction

Speech Emotion Recognition (SER) research has largely relied on acted emotion. This project instead studies *naturally expressed* post-class affect in Computer Science students. Each participant says one Bisaya word of their choosing and then reports how they actually feel. The self-report, not the meaning of the word and not a listener's impression, is the reference label ("Kapoy" ≠ automatically sad).

The computational question is whether *how* the word is spoken (its acoustic and prosodic realisation) contains information about that self-reported state.

## 2. Research Objectives

1. Determine the affective states reported by CS students immediately after class.
2. Examine the acoustic and prosodic characteristics of short Bisaya post-class responses.
3. Investigate whether acoustic/prosodic features can classify self-reported affective states.
4. Compare appropriate machine learning models for Bisaya affect recognition.
5. Explore relationships between post-class affect and educational context (class activity, year level, session).

## 3. Research Questions

| RQ | Question (protocol) | Addressed in Group 3 |
|---|---|---|
| RQ1 | What affective states do students report immediately after class? | §7.1 |
| RQ2 | How does affect vary by year level, class activity and session? | **Not answerable within Group 3**: all three are constant (§7.3); requires the consolidated class dataset |
| RQ3 | Which acoustic/prosodic characteristics accompany different self-reported states? | §7.2 |
| RQ4 | To what extent can ML classify self-reported affect from acoustic features? | §8 |
| RQ5 | Which model performs best? | §8.3 |

## 4. Methodology

### 4.1 Participants

The assigned population is Second-Year CS students (protocol §IV). The Group 3 metadata lists 40 participants, Y2-041 to Y2-080, every one recorded as 2nd year. Recordings were supplied for 40 of them (as CS2B_v2_wav_16k copies; see §4.3). The analysis set comprises the **40 participants** with a usable recording. Every participant contributes exactly one observation.

### 4.2 Research Ethics

The metadata records informed consent ('Yes') for all 40 participants. **No consent documentation (consent log or institutional clearance) has been supplied.** Protocol §VI makes it a requirement before the data can be used for publication, so the results in this report must not be disseminated until it is verified.

Participants are identified only by pseudonymous codes. The raw videos (faces, possible GPS tags) are kept locally and never copied into the analysis. Only audio is processed, and location metadata is never extracted.

### 4.3 Data Collection

Every metadata row records Class Activity 'Lecture' and Session 'Afternoon–Evening' (subject: Environmental Science for 40 rows, blank for 0).

The analysed files are converted copies and carry no capture time. The capture times of the original recordings, audited before the switch, were consistent with the recorded session, except for the originals of 5 files, which have a different configuration or a much later capture time (§6). The time boundary between sessions was not documented in the supplied material.

**Audio source (group decision, 2026-10-04):** the analysis uses the `CS2B_v2_wav_16k` delivery, 40 WAV files (PCM 16-bit, mono, 16 kHz), one per participant, converted and trimmed by a group member from the smartphone recordings (iPhone 17, MOV). The original recordings are archived in `data/raw/` and not analysed. 31 files are copies of an original; 9 have no verified original (Y2-053, Y2-071, Y2-074, Y2-075, Y2-076, Y2-077, Y2-078, Y2-079, Y2-080); 3 contain inserted digital silence or clipping (Y2-076, Y2-077, Y2-078). Provenance: `reports/supplied_audio_audit.md`.

### 4.4 Natural Bisaya Speech Procedure

Participants were asked to choose one word closest to their reaction and say it naturally. The protocol lists Salamat, Ambot, Grabe, Lisod, Sayon, Lingaw and Kapoy.

In Group 3, 21 of 40 recorded words are on that list (Kapoy, Salamat, Lingaw, Grabe) and 19 are not (most frequent: Nalipay, Katulgon, Lipay, Okay). 0 rows have no recorded word. Whether off-list words are acceptable needs an instructor ruling. They are kept here because the word is never a model input.

### 4.5 Self-Reported Affect

Immediately after the recording, each participant described how they felt and rated valence (1 very unpleasant – 5 very pleasant) and arousal (1 very low – 5 very high). These ratings are the reference labels.

Y2-076's arousal rating is struck through in the sheet and is not used. Y2-076 can therefore enter only the valence analyses.

### 4.6 Audio Processing

1. **Audio QA of the supplied files:** peak, clipping, DC offset, level and inserted digital silence.
2. **Standardisation:** the files are already WAV PCM 16-bit mono 16 kHz; ffmpeg passes the samples through unchanged (checked bit-identical). The pipeline adds no filtering, denoising, normalisation, pitch or speed change; the supplier's trimming and edits cannot be undone.
3. **Target-utterance localisation.** The clips contain continuous hallway babble and sometimes other speech, so the participant's word was located as the dominant short-time-energy event. This is deterministic and blind to labels. Segments touching the clip edge, longer than 1.5 s, or with a competing event within 3 dB are flagged.
4. **One file per participant.** Where a participant was recorded more than once, the delivery contains one take (the latest, according to the audit), which is used as supplied.
5. **Naming:** `ParticipantCode_YearLevel_Session_Word.wav`. `PM` is assumed for Afternoon–Evening, and `UNVERIFIED` is used where no word was recorded.

### 4.7 Acoustic Feature Extraction

For each located utterance, 108 features were computed: duration and voicing (3); F0 from Praat autocorrelation pitch (mean, SD, median, minimum, maximum, IQR in Hz; semitone SD, range and slope) (9); RMS energy in dBFS (6); zero-crossing rate (6); 13 MFCCs with Δ and ΔΔ (mean and SD each: 78); spectral centroid, bandwidth and roll-off (6).

Praat was used instead of librosa pYIN, whose voicing decisions were unstable in this noise (see documentation). F0 in Hz mainly reflects voice type, because no speaker baseline exists.

### 4.8 Machine Learning Methods

- **Inputs:** acoustic features only. Spoken word, feeling text, year, subject, session, class activity, participant code and file names are excluded, and the training script refuses to run otherwise.
- **Targets:** derived groupings of the participants' own ratings. A task is modelled only if every class has at least 5 participants. Modelled: arousal_3 (primary), valence_2 (primary), arousal_2 (secondary). Not modelled (too few participants in a class): valence_5, arousal_5, valence_3.
- **Models:** DummyClassifier (majority; stratified), L2 logistic regression, RBF SVM and random forest, each in a Pipeline of median imputation and standardisation (no scaler for the forest).
- **Imbalance:** class weights; no resampling.
- **Tuning:** small grids, tuned only inside training folds.

### 4.9 Evaluation Strategy

- **Cross-validation:** speaker-independent StratifiedGroupKFold grouped by participant (5 folds), repeated 10 times. Every split is verified to share no participant.
- **Metrics:** accuracy, balanced accuracy, macro precision, recall and F1, per-class metrics and confusion matrices.
- **Uncertainty and chance:** a participant-level bootstrap gives 95% intervals. A label-permutation test (500 permutations of the full nested procedure) checks each model against chance, with Holm adjustment.
- **Model comparison:** corrected repeated k-fold t-test (Nadeau & Bengio, 2003).
- **Sensitivity analyses:** the same design after removing, in turn: config-B/capture-outlier recordings, segmentation-critical recordings, files without a verified original recording, edited or clipped files.

## 7. Exploratory Analysis

### 7.1 Self-reported affect (RQ1)

Valence was mostly neutral to pleasant (analysis set: 1: 1, 2: 2, 3: 17, 4: 11, 5: 9) and arousal mostly moderate to high (1: 3, 2: 6, 3: 15, 4: 12, 5: 4). Only 3 participants in the analysis set reported unpleasant valence (1–2). Valence and arousal were strongly positively correlated (ρ = 0.72, p = 1.3e-07, n = 40): lower valence tended to co-occur with lower arousal.

### 7.2 Acoustic characteristics by self-reported affect (RQ3)

Across 108 features, 0 correlated with arousal and 1 with valence after Benjamini–Hochberg correction. The strongest associations were delta_mfcc_13_std with arousal (ρ = +0.39, q = 0.365) and rms_db_iqr with valence (ρ = -0.54, q = 0.032).

Among the six pre-specified prosodic features (F0 median, F0 range, RMS level, duration, spectral centroid, voiced ratio), the strongest association with arousal was spectral_centroid_hz_mean (ρ = +0.35, p = 0.027) and with valence rms_db_mean (ρ = +0.37, p = 0.017); none passed FDR correction (see `reports/exploratory_analysis.md`, Fig. 9–10).

### 7.3 Educational context (RQ2)

Year level (2nd year), class activity (Lecture) and session (Afternoon–Evening) are constant across Group 3, and subject is one value or blank. Their relationship with affect **cannot be estimated** from these data; this requires the consolidated class dataset.

## 9. Lexically Controlled Analysis

Only *Kapoy* had enough recordings (15) and rating variation for a same-word comparison. Within *Kapoy*, 0 of 12 feature–rating correlations passed FDR correction. Within-word correlations had the same sign as in the full sample in 17% of tests. With n = 15 (10 report valence 3, 6 report arousal 3), these estimates are descriptive only.

The lexical-confound probe separated *Kapoy* from other words with balanced accuracy 0.689 (permutation p = 0.072); acoustic features did not reliably carry word identity in this sample. Word choice was associated with the ratings (valence_2: p = 0.001, Cramér's V = 0.57; arousal_3: p = 0.005, Cramér's V = 0.51).

Out-of-fold accuracy of the affect models, averaged over the three learned models: arousal_2: 0.66 for Kapoy vs 0.42 for other words; arousal_3: 0.42 for Kapoy vs 0.35 for other words; valence_2: 0.68 for Kapoy vs 0.68 for other words.

Some full-sample associations change sign once the word is held constant (rms_db_mean with valence: ρ = +0.37 in the full sample but -0.47 within Kapoy). Those associations are therefore at least partly lexical.

Both conditions for a lexical confound (word identifiable from acoustics, and word associated with the self-reports) were not jointly met at p < 0.05 in this sample.

Full detail: `reports/lexical_control_analysis.md`.

## 10. Discussion

**Observations.**
- 40 of 40 participants are analysed from the CS2B_v2_wav_16k copies (9 without a verified original, 3 edited or clipped); 0 words are missing; 5 files are copies of recordings with a different configuration.
- The recordings are short clips in a noisy, multi-speaker environment.
- Self-reports cluster at neutral-to-pleasant valence (3–5: 37 of 40) and moderate-to-high arousal (3–5: 31 of 40).

**Statistical results.**
- Valence and arousal co-vary strongly (ρ = 0.72).
- After FDR correction, 0 features are associated with arousal and 1 with valence.
- No feature differs significantly between recording configurations.

**Model performance.**
- No learned model exceeded the label-permutation null after Holm correction (all adjusted p ≥ 0.05; smallest unadjusted p = 0.0060, before correcting for 9 tests). Before correction, 1 of 9 tests had p < 0.05 (Random forest on valence_2: p = 0.006). If no model carried any signal, about 0.45 such results would be expected by chance across these tests, and none survives the correction.
- Highest point estimates: valence_2: Random forest 0.703 (chance 0.50); arousal_2: Random forest 0.554 (chance 0.50); arousal_3: Random forest 0.410 (chance 0.33).
- Bootstrap intervals are wide and overlap chance-level baselines.

**Interpretation.**
- Within this pilot dataset, the evidence that the speech signal of a single word predicts an unseen student's self-reported affect is weak at best.
- Three factors plausibly limit any signal:
  1. a small, label-sparse sample (very few unpleasant or low-arousal reports);
  2. heavy background babble and automatic utterance localisation;
  3. single-word utterances that give little prosodic material.
- Lexical content could still be absorbed by an acoustic model, although the confound conditions were not jointly significant in this sample.
- Recording configuration remains a possible confound (5 files), although no feature differs significantly in this analysis.
- These are associations in a small observational sample. Nothing here shows that classes, activities or words *cause* any affective state.
- A negative or null result at this sample size is informative for the class study: it argues for the consolidated dataset, quieter recording, and verified segmentation.

## 11. Limitations

1. **Small sample:** n = 40 meets the protocol minimum of 40, but only correlations of about |ρ| ≥ 0.44 are reliably detectable (80% power, two-sided α = 0.05), and 9 of the 40 observations rest on copies without a verified original.
2. **Class imbalance and sparse categories:** unpleasant valence n = 3; valence_5, arousal_5, valence_3 could not be modelled; derived groupings merge categories.
3. **Single-word utterances** (0.14–1.79 s located segments) carry limited prosodic information.
4. **Naturally occurring noise:** background voices detected in 16 of 40 selected clips; low utterance-to-background ratio (< 10 dB) in 10.
5. **Automatic segmentation** (segment boundaries not yet verified by listening); 14 recordings have segmentation-critical flags.
6. **Device/setting variability:** 5 files are copies of recordings with a different audio configuration; no feature differs significantly here, but the test has little power. F0 in Hz is dominated by voice type (no speaker baseline).
7. **Limited contextual variation:** one year level, one activity, one session; RQ2 is not answerable within Group 3.
8. **Possible lexical influence:** 19 of 40 words are off the protocol list and words differ phonetically, so acoustic features can encode word identity.
9. **Self-report uncertainty:** single-item ratings; 20 rows with feeling text identical to the word; 0 rows without a description; 0 struck-through ratings.
10. **The analysed audio is not the original recordings:** by the group's decision the analysis uses the CS2B_v2_wav_16k copies (trimmed 16 kHz WAVs made by a group member), so capture times and native-format QA are lost; 9 files have no verified original (Y2-053, Y2-071, Y2-074, Y2-075, Y2-076, Y2-077, Y2-078, Y2-079, Y2-080) and 3 contain inserted digital silence or clipping (Y2-076, Y2-077, Y2-078). Sensitivity analyses exclude them. Where a participant was recorded more than once, the delivery's take is used.
11. **No demographic variables were collected** (the protocol allows optional variables only when approved), so speaker characteristics such as sex confound F0.
12. **Consent documentation not supplied;** dissemination is blocked until it is verified.
13. **Limited generalisability:** one class session, one device model; a pilot study.

## 12. Conclusion

The Group 3 pipeline is complete and reproducible: data audit, metadata cleaning, audio standardisation and quality control, feature extraction, exploratory analysis, speaker-independent machine learning, evaluation, lexical control and validation. It produced a documented dataset of 40 observations.

No learned model exceeded the label-permutation null after Holm correction (all adjusted p ≥ 0.05; smallest unadjusted p = 0.0060, before correcting for 9 tests). Before correction, 1 of 9 tests had p < 0.05 (Random forest on valence_2: p = 0.006). If no model carried any signal, about 0.45 such results would be expected by chance across these tests, and none survives the correction. Within this pilot dataset, the results therefore do not support a claim that the system can recognise post-class affect from speech.

They do identify concrete requirements for the consolidated study: reach the planned sample, record in a quieter location with one consistent device setting, verify the target utterance by listening, collect more low-valence and low-arousal responses, and supply consent documentation.
